issues.legal_issue: A joint promisee cannot enforce the original contract in its unchanged form where the other joint promisee has settled and rescinded his part of the contract, in circumstances making the authorities permitting one joint promisee to sue inapplicable.
material_facts: The agreement was made jointly by two purchasers for land to be developed together with adjoining land under a common layout.
One purchaser sued the owners for refund of his advance and damages, then entered into a compromise with them that was recorded by a court.
The remaining purchaser was a party to that suit, appeared through counsel, and did not oppose the compromise.
The remaining purchaser did not immediately sue for specific performance after the compromise; he had first sought a mandatory injunction.
issues.conclusion: The agreement could not be specifically enforced in its original form after the compromise had been recorded and part of the contract had been worked out. The authorities allowing one joint promisee to sue despite another's refusal to join did not apply to these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court proceeded on the basis that a joint promisee may in principle sue for enforcement even if another joint promisee refuses to join, as recognized in Jahar Roy v. Premji Bhimji Mansata and the authorities discussed there. But that principle presupposes enforcement of the original contract as made. A settlement and court-recorded compromise that rescinds and works out part of the contract can make enforcement in that original form unavailable. Section 45 of the Indian Contract Act was discussed in Jahar Roy in relation to devolution of joint rights, but the present decision turned on the effect of the compromise and the particular circumstances.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and joint_promisees_contract and (co_promisee_settled_and_rescinded_part or co_promisee_claim_worked_out) and remaining_claimant_did_not_oppose_settlement

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.joint_promisees_contract: The contract was made jointly for multiple promisees.
predicates.co_promisee_settled_and_rescinded_part: One joint promisee settled with the other contracting party in a way that rescinded or resolved that promisee's part of the contract.
predicates.co_promisee_claim_worked_out: The claim of one joint promisee had been settled or otherwise worked out, so the original contract could no longer be enforced unchanged.
predicates.remaining_claimant_did_not_oppose_settle: The remaining claimant was involved in the proceeding in which the settlement was recorded but did not oppose it.
predicates.original_contract_not_enforceable_in_sam: The original contract cannot be specifically enforced in its unchanged form.

issues.definition: If a specific-performance suit concerns a contract made jointly for multiple promisees and one promisee's part has been settled or worked out, the remaining claimant's failure to oppose that settlement means the original contract is not enforceable in the same form.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance is discretionary, and a claimant's conduct, delay, and failure to act consistently with the contract may justify refusing that relief even when the claim is brought within the limitation period.
material_facts: The contract required completion within a specified period after release of a tentative layout and provided for interest on unpaid purchase money after the stipulated period.
The purchasers pursued a common layout for the contracted land and adjoining land, but roads required for final approval were not constructed.
The remaining purchaser did not promptly insist on a separate layout or allege breach by the owners, and raised the separate-layout position in response to the owners' notice.
After the other purchaser settled with the owners, the remaining purchaser did not promptly sue for specific performance and had first brought a suit for mandatory injunction.
The trial court had not addressed the significance of the claimant's conduct in exercising the discretionary jurisdiction to grant specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to grant specific performance in the circumstances and upheld the refusal of that discretionary relief. It emphasized that no absolute rule governs such cases and that the claimant's conduct and the facts of the case matter.
issues.legal_principle: Specific performance is discretionary and the discretion must be exercised judiciously; a claimant's conduct and approach to the court with clean hands are material, as stated in Mohammadia Cooperative Building Society Ltd. v. Lakshmi Srinivasa Cooperative Building Society Ltd. Sanjana M. Wig v. Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. recognizes that the exercise of discretion depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. Although time is not invariably of the essence for contracts concerning immovable property, contractual time stipulations cannot be ignored, as explained in K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan. Mademsetty Satyanarayana v. G. Yellogi Rao recognizes that prolonged inaction, particularly when accompanied by circumstances making relief inequitable, may defeat specific performance. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd. does not establish a universal rule; each case must be considered on its facts.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant sought specific performance of a contract.
predicates.claimant_delayed_specific_performance_cl: The claimant did not promptly seek specific performance after the relevant contractual dispute or change in circumstances arose.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_act_consistently_with: The claimant's actions or omissions were inconsistent with timely performance or with the position later advanced in support of specific performance.
predicates.claimant_conduct_makes_relief_inequitabl: In the circumstances of the case, the claimant's conduct makes an order for specific performance inequitable.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a specific-performance suit delays seeking that relief, fails to act consistently with the contract, and thereby makes relief inequitable, specific performance is refused.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not use its discretionary appellate jurisdiction to disturb a High Court's refusal of specific performance where that refusal is an exercise of discretion and the trial court did not address the relevant conduct.
material_facts: The High Court reversed the trial court's decree for specific performance and refused that relief.
The trial court had not considered the claimant's conduct when exercising its discretion.
The appeal asked the Supreme Court to interfere with the High Court's discretionary decision.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court's exercise of discretion and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, particularly because the High Court had exercised discretion and the trial court had not addressed the relevant conduct. The judgment also relies on the principle that discretionary relief must be exercised judiciously, as discussed in Mohammadia Cooperative Building Society Ltd. v. Lakshmi Srinivasa Cooperative Building Society Ltd.

predicates.article_136_appeal_in_specific_performan: An appeal under discretionary Supreme Court jurisdiction concerns a claim for specific performance.
predicates.high_court_refused_discretionary_relief: The High Court refused the requested relief through an exercise of discretion.
predicates.trial_court_did_not_consider_relevant_co: The trial court did not consider the claimant's relevant conduct when deciding whether to grant discretionary relief.
predicates.supreme_court_declines_interference: The Supreme Court declines to disturb the High Court's decision.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning specific performance, when the High Court has refused relief as a matter of discretion and the trial court did not consider relevant conduct, the Supreme Court declines to disturb the High Court's decision.
